claim: Alpha-band oscillations are in the 8-12 Hz frequency range.
source: Previous research has associated alpha-band [8–12 Hz] oscillations with inhibitory functions
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the definition of alpha-band oscillations.

claim: Visual attention increases alpha-band power in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the attended location.

claim: Alpha oscillations positively correlate with visual perception.
source: other studies demonstrated that alpha oscillations positively correlate with visual perception

claim: There are two functionally distinct alpha-band oscillations propagating in different directions.

claim: Three datasets of human participants performing a covert visual attention task were analyzed (one new dataset with N = 16, two previously published datasets with N = 16 and N = 31).
source: We analyzed EEG recordings from three datasets of human participants performing a covert visual attention task (one new dataset with N = 16, two previously published datasets with N = 16 and N = 31).
evidence: Direct statement about the datasets used in the study.

claim: Allocating attention to one hemifield increases top-down alpha-band waves propagating from frontal to occipital regions ipsilateral to the attended location.
source: allocating attention to one hemifield increases top-down alpha-band waves propagating from frontal to occipital regions ipsilateral to the attended location, both with and without visual stimulation
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Top-down alpha-band waves occur both with and without visual stimulation.
source: allocating attention to one hemifield increases top-down alpha-band waves propagating from frontal to occipital regions ipsilateral to the attended location, both with and without visual stimulation
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Top-down oscillatory waves correlate positively with alpha-band power in frontal and occipital regions.
source: These top-down oscillatory waves correlate positively with alpha-band power in frontal and occipital regions.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the study.

claim: Different alpha-band waves propagate from occipital to frontal regions and contralateral to the attended location.
source: Yet, different alpha-band waves propagate from occipital to frontal regions and contralateral to the attended location.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Forward waves were present only during visual stimulation.

claim: Brain oscillations orchestrate neuronal activity at distinct temporal and spatial scales.
source: Brain oscillations are related to several cognitive functions, as they orchestrate neuronal activity at distinct temporal and spatial scales (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Buzsáki, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alpha-band oscillations are the most prevailing rhythms in electrophysiological (EEG) recordings.
source: Alpha-band oscillations [8–12 Hz] are the most prevailing rhythms in electrophysiological (EEG) recordings, spreading through most cortical regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Alpha-band oscillations spread through most cortical regions.
source: Alpha-band oscillations [8–12 Hz] are the most prevailing rhythms in electrophysiological (EEG) recordings, spreading through most cortical regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about alpha oscillations.

claim: Alpha-band oscillations might filter sensory information, regulating excitation and inhibition of sensory-specific brain regions.
source: some studies showed that alpha-band oscillations might filter sensory information, regulating excitation and inhibition of sensory-specific brain regions (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Mathewson et al., 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Sadaghiani and Kleinschmidt, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alpha oscillations are interpreted as a top-down mechanism involved in inhibitory control and timing of cortical processing.
source: researchers interpreted alpha oscillations as a top-down mechanism involved in inhibitory control and timing of cortical processing (Klimesch et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Alpha oscillations modulate cortical excitability.
source: as well as modulating cortical excitability (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Mathewson et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The phase of alpha-band oscillation affects visual perception.
source: Experimental studies corroborated this hypothesis, demonstrating how the phase of alpha-band oscillation affects visual perception (Busch et al., 2009; Fakche et al., 2022; but see also Ruzzoli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Visual attention causes hemispheric modulation in occipital regions with an increase of alpha power ipsilateral to the attended hemifield and a corresponding decrease contralaterally.
source: Another highly replicated result regarding the inhibitory role of alpha oscillations consists in the hemispheric modulation in occipital regions associated with visual attention, having an increase of power ipsilateral to the attended hemifield, and a corresponding decrease contralaterally (Worden et al., 2000; Sauseng et al., 2005; Kelly et al., 2006; Thut et al., 2006; Händel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Alpha-band oscillations in occipital and parietal regions are related to perceptual processing and visual memory.
source: other experimental studies have related alpha-band oscillations in occipital and parietal regions to perceptual processing and visual memory (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012; VanRullen, 2016; Pang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The visual system reverberates sensory information in the alpha-band for as long as 1 s in 'perceptual echoes'.
source: reverse-correlation techniques reveal that the visual system reverberates sensory information in the alpha-band for as long as 1 s, in what has been dubbed 'perceptual echoes' (VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research using reverse-correlation techniques.

claim: Perceptual echoes reflect the input's precise time course.
source: these echoes are a clear signature of sensory processing as they reflect the input's precise time course
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Perceptual echoes are modulated by attention.
source: these echoes are a clear signature of sensory processing as they reflect the input's precise time course, are modulated by attention
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perceptual echoes have been dissociated from inhibitory alpha power modulation.
source: have been dissociated from inhibitory alpha power modulation (VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012; VanRullen, 2016; Brüers and VanRullen, 2018; Schwenk et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual perception modulates alpha waves, with forward waves during visual stimulation and backward waves when the stimulus was off.
source: in which we showed how visual perception modulates alpha waves, that is forward waves during visual stimulation, backward waves when the stimulus was off
evidence: This refers to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Distinct alpha-band oscillations are related to specific cognitive processes.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alpha-band oscillatory waves propagate in both directions during visual stimulation.
source: confirming previous experimental studies (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Pang et al., 2020), we found that alpha-band oscillatory waves propagate in both directions during visual stimulation
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that confirms previous research.

claim: Theta (4-7 Hz) waves propagate mostly bottom-up from occipital to frontal regions.
source: theta (4–7 Hz) and high-beta/gamma (24–45 Hz) bands propagate mostly bottom-up from occipital to frontal regions

claim: High-beta/gamma (24-45 Hz) waves propagate mostly bottom-up from occipital to frontal regions.
source: theta (4–7 Hz) and high-beta/gamma (24–45 Hz) bands propagate mostly bottom-up from occipital to frontal regions
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral profile analysis in the study.

claim: Low-beta (13-23 Hz) waves flow in the top-down direction.
source: low-beta (13–23 Hz) waves flow in the top-down direction
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral profile analysis in the study.

claim: Higher frequency bands (high-beta/gamma) have been associated with forward processing.
source: this pattern of results confirms previous studies using different methods, in which higher frequency bands (i.e., high-beta/gamma) have been associated with forward processing, whereas low-beta and alpha frequencies have been related to top-down processing (Bastos et al., 2012; Bastos et al., 2015; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Michalareas et al., 2016; but see also Schneider et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low-beta and alpha frequencies have been related to top-down processing.
source: this pattern of results confirms previous studies using different methods, in which higher frequency bands (i.e., high-beta/gamma) have been associated with forward processing, whereas low-beta and alpha frequencies have been related to top-down processing (Bastos et al., 2012; Bastos et al., 2015; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Michalareas et al., 2016; but see also Schneider et al., 2021b).

source: the results support a significant correlation between backward waves and alpha power in the hemisphere contralateral to the attended location (BF10 = 10.7 and BF10 = 7.4 for occipital and frontal regions, respectively

source: we surmised that the lateralization effect we reported in the forward waves in our dataset (absent in the Foster dataset) is related to the steady visual stimulation during the attentional allocation, in line with our previous results demonstrating that oscillatory bottom-up waves reflect sensory processing (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Pang et al., 2020).

source: A Bayesian ANOVA reveals no difference between targets and distractors (EVENT: BF10 = 0.206, error ~1%)

claim: A missed target is related to an increase in backward waves contralateral to the attended location.

claim: Missed targets are due to a failure of attentional allocation rather than sensory processing.
source: The opposite pattern for hits versus misses, already visible before the target onset, suggests that missed targets are due to a failure of attentional allocation rather than sensory processing

claim: Selective attention modulates alpha-band oscillations in occipital and parietal regions.

claim: Attention modulates oscillations traveling from occipital to frontal regions only in the presence of visual stimulation.

source: this attentional modulation involved both an decrease of alpha waves contralateral to the attended location, and an ipsilateral increase.

claim: Two different sources of alpha-band oscillations exist during a multisensory task: one in visual areas reflecting the 'spotlight of attention' that decreases linearly with increasing attention, and another in parietal regions indicating attentional efforts.
source: A recent study from Sokoliuk et al., 2019 demonstrated two different sources of alpha-band oscillations during a multisensory task: one, located in visual areas, reflects the 'spotlight of attention' and decreases linearly with increasing attention, whereas another one indicates attentional efforts and occurs in parietal regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Parietal, but not occipital alpha-band oscillations are responsible for the oscillatory reverberation causing the 'triple-flash' illusion.
source: Gulbinaite et al. also demonstrated that parietal, but not occipital alpha-band oscillations are responsible for the oscillatory reverberation causing the 'triple-flash' illusion (Gulbinaite et al., 2017).

claim: Alpha-band oscillations play a causal role in top-down but not bottom-up attention.
source: The authors interpreted their results as evidence supporting the hypothesis that alpha-band oscillations play a causal role in top-down but not bottom-up attention (Schuhmann et al., 2019; Kasten et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Top-down processes, as reflected by backward waves, drive the well-documented hemispheric asymmetries reported in the literature.
source: Our findings support the hypothesis that top-down processes, as reflected by backward waves, drive the well-documented hemispheric asymmetries reported in the literature (Händel et al., 2011; Klimesch, 2012; Waldhauser et al., 2012; Peylo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Target enhancement is reflected in an increase in the contralateral alpha-band waves processing the target and propagating forward.

evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: Alpha waves are involved in both distractor suppression (via ipsilateral top-down inhibitory feedback) and target enhancement (via contralateral bottom-up alpha-band waves).
source: Our results thus support the hypothesis that alpha waves are involved in both distractor suppression (via ipsilateral top-down inhibitory feedback) and target enhancement (via contralateral bottom-up alpha-band waves).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the findings of the study.

claim: A simple multilevel hierarchical model based on Predictive Coding principles and implementing biologically plausible constraints gives rise to oscillatory traveling waves propagating both forward and backward.
source: We demonstrated that a simple multilevel hierarchical model based on Predictive Coding (PC) principles and implementing biologically plausible constraints (temporal delays between brain areas and neural time constants) gives rise to oscillatory traveling waves propagating both forward and backward.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Predictive Coding model is consistent with the two-dipole hypothesis.
source: This model is also consistent with the two-dipole hypothesis (Zhigalov and Jensen, 2022), considering the interaction between the parietal and occipital areas (i.e., a model of two hierarchical levels).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the PC model with the two-dipole hypothesis.

claim: In the Predictive Coding framework, top-down connections have an inhibitory function, suppressing the activity predicted by higher-level regions.
source: This hypothesis is in line with the PC framework, in which top-down connections have an inhibitory function, suppressing the activity predicted by higher-level regions (Huang and Rao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on Predictive Coding.

claim: Predictive Coding can be reformulated as a model of biased competition in visual attention.
source: Spratling proposed a simple reformulation of the terms in the PC equations that could describe it as a model of biased competition in visual attention, thus corroborating the interpretation of our finding within the PC framework (Spratling, 2008; Spratling, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Top-down waves prevail in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the attended location and are related to inhibitory functions.
source: Top-down waves prevail in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the attended location and are related to inhibitory functions
